videoIdeas.title: The 3-second rule that kills your public speaking
videoIdeas.hook: Most people lose the room in the first sentence — and they don't even know they did it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Listicle/tactical breakdowns are the format carrying this niche right now — Daanish's '5 careers' hit 160k and Birdtart's networking-questions video did nearly a million. I have zero tactical public speaking content; it's a pillar I claim but never actually teach. This fills that gap with a concrete, saveable tip.
videoIdeas.script: Most people lose the room in the first sentence — and they don't even know they did it. They walk up and say 'Hi, um, so, today I'm going to talk about…' You've already told the audience to check their phones. Here's the fix. Open with a line that costs them something to look away from. A number. A claim. A question they can't answer in their head. 'Ninety percent of you will quit this in a week.' Now they're listening, because they want to know if they're the ninety percent. You earn the boring stuff — the intro, the context, the 'my name is' — after you've taken the room, not before. Nobody owes you their attention. You take it in the first three seconds or you spend the rest of the talk begging for it back.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-shot, plain wall or in front of an empty lecture hall / stage. Smart casual, calm energy — you're not hyping, you're explaining. Hands used sparingly for emphasis.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'You lost the room here ↓' overlaid on a clip of you mumbling a weak 'um, so, today…' opener, then hard cut to you upright and direct.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence: start already talking, no intro, as if we caught the middle of a lesson
On-screen countdown '3…2…1… gone' ticking over a crowd losing interest
Split screen: weak opener vs strong opener side by side

videoIdeas.title: Why your du'a for confidence isn't working
videoIdeas.hook: You keep praying for confidence. Allah keeps sending you situations that build it. You keep avoiding them.
videoIdeas.rationale: Dinoo's 'You can pray and still need help — both can be true' did 20k on a short, punchy faith-meets-reality take. My single best post was the Majid Freeman one (289 likes) — faith framed with action. This merges that proven angle with a mindset lesson, which is cheaper to produce than my history essays and more repeatable.
videoIdeas.script: You keep praying for confidence. And Allah keeps sending you situations that build it — and you keep avoiding them. You asked for courage, then said no to the presentation, the awkward conversation, the thing that scared you. That wasn't the obstacle to your du'a. That was the answer to it. Tawakkul was never 'pray and wait for the feeling.' Tie your camel, then trust. The feeling of confidence comes after the action, not before it. You don't get brave and then do hard things. You do hard things, repeatedly, badly at first — and the bravery is the residue. Stop waiting to feel ready. Ready is a reward, not a starting point.

visuals.setting: Closer, more intimate framing. Softer light, maybe seated. Lower, slower delivery — this one lands on tone, not volume. Neutral clothing.
visuals.visualHook: Bold on-screen text: 'Your du'a was answered. You just said no to it.' held in silence for a beat before you speak.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: open with 'Harsh truth about your du'a —' then pause
Cold open on the single line 'Ready is a reward, not a starting point' then rewind to build to it
Text-only black screen hook that forces a read before the face appears

videoIdeas.title: 5 things weak leaders say
videoIdeas.hook: Five sentences that tell me you'll never be trusted to lead anything.
videoIdeas.rationale: The '5 X' countable format is the single most reliable winner in this data — Daanish ran it twice (160k, 30k). I've never done a listicle and I've never posted pure leadership tactics. This is the clearest format gap I have, applied to my strongest pillar.
videoIdeas.script: Five sentences that tell me you'll never be trusted to lead anything. One: 'That's not my job.' In a team, everything that affects the outcome is your job. Two: 'I told you so.' A leader fixes the problem in the room, not their own ego. Three: 'Whatever you guys want.' That's not humility, that's abdication — people followed you to decide. Four: 'It's not my fault.' Maybe not. But it's your responsibility, and those are different words for a reason. Five: 'We've always done it this way.' That's the sentence every dying organisation says right before it dies. Leadership isn't a title they hand you. It's the words you stop allowing yourself to say.

visuals.setting: Mid-shot, confident upright posture, clean background. Each point gets a sharp cut — slight reframe or jump cut so it feels like a list. Measured, authoritative energy.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen numbered counter '1/5' appearing with the first line, text of each weak phrase stamped on screen in quotes as you say it.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on number 5 (the strongest) then 'but first, number one'
On-screen text punchline: the quoted weak sentences flash before you speak each
Finger count on camera synced to each point for rhythm

videoIdeas.title: How a 19-year-old conquered Spain (and what it teaches you about fear)
videoIdeas.hook: Tariq bin Ziyad burned his own ships so his men couldn't retreat. Most of you won't even delete one app.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Tariq bin Ziyad / Andalusia post was my #1 by views (437). The history angle is clearly mine and clearly works, but the original stopped at history. Reframing it into a mindset lesson makes it repeatable and gives people a reason to save and share, not just admire.
videoIdeas.script: Tariq bin Ziyad burned his own ships so his men couldn't retreat. Most of you won't even delete one app. When he landed in Spain in 711, he was outnumbered badly. So he removed the one thing killing his army's focus — the option to go back. No ships, no retreat, no 'maybe we'll try again next year.' Full attention, because full attention was the only option left. You're not losing because you lack ability. You're losing because you've kept every exit open. The side hustle you 'might' do. The deen you'll get serious about 'later.' You've left the ships in the water. Burn them. Commitment isn't a feeling — it's the deliberate removal of the escape route.

visuals.setting: Same tone as your history post that worked — direct to camera, serious. Could intercut with a still map or coastline B-roll. Darker, cinematic grade suits the subject.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'He burned the ships. You won't delete one app.' over an image of burning ships / a coastline before cutting to you.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on the vivid historical image with text, voice starts over it
Pattern interrupt: 'This is a 1300-year-old productivity hack' then the story
End-card hook teased at the start: 'the ships are the point — wait for it'

videoIdeas.title: Nobody is coming to give you the mic
videoIdeas.hook: You're waiting to be picked. That's the whole problem.
videoIdeas.rationale: Birdtart's near-1M video was pure tactical agency ('questions to connect with people'). The winning thread across top posts is empowerment-through-action, not inspiration. This is a short, high-share leadership/agency piece with no production cost — just you and a clear idea.
videoIdeas.script: You're waiting to be picked. That's the whole problem. Waiting for the manager to notice you, the teacher to call on you, the community to hand you a role. Here's what nobody tells you: the people running things aren't more qualified than you. They just stopped asking permission. The brother leading the halaqa started it because the chairs were empty and he sat at the front. Authority in most rooms is just the person who moved first while everyone else waited to be invited. Nobody is coming to give you the mic. Pick it up. Worst case, you learn you weren't ready — and now you know exactly what to fix. Best case, you were the leader the whole time and just needed to act like it.

visuals.setting: Standing, energetic but controlled. Plain or urban background. Slightly faster pace — this is a push, not a reflection. Direct eye contact throughout.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'Stop waiting to be picked.' slammed on screen in the first frame, no music intro.
otherHookIdeas: Prop hook: hold an actual mic and set it down in frame on the line 'pick it up'
Cold open mid-rant with no greeting
On-screen text punchline reveal: 'authority = whoever moved first'

videoIdeas.title: The red pill is selling you weakness dressed as strength
videoIdeas.hook: They told you to be a high-value man. Then handed you the mindset of a scared one.
videoIdeas.rationale: Dinoo's red-pill rebuttal did 23k with 211 comments — the highest comment count in the competitor set. Response/counter-narrative content drives discussion, and this is squarely on-brand for a self-development account for young Muslim men. I have no commentary content; this fills a conversation-driving gap.
videoIdeas.script: They told you to be a high-value man. Then handed you the mindset of a scared one. Think about what the red pill actually teaches: never be vulnerable, never commit, assume everyone's using you, keep score in every relationship. That's not strength. That's a man who's been hurt and decided to call his armour a personality. Real strength is softer and harder at the same time — soft enough to love people openly, hard enough to hold a standard when it costs you. The Prophet ﷺ was the gentlest man in any room and the bravest. Those weren't in tension. The grifters selling you 'alpha' have never built anything that lasts — not a marriage, not a community, not themselves. Don't take wealth advice from the broke. Don't take strength advice from the bitter.

visuals.setting: Direct to camera, grounded and calm — the strength is in not being loud. Neutral background. Let the content be the edge, not the delivery.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'Being 'alpha' is just fear with good marketing.' before you speak.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: 'I'm going to lose some followers for this' then the take
Cold open on the Prophet ﷺ line to anchor it in deen early
On-screen text contrast: 'armour ≠ personality' stamped mid-video

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your #1 by views (437) and it's no accident — a specific historical hook ('In 711 AD, Christians were begging Muslims to liberate them') is concrete and surprising, which is exactly the kind of opener that stops a scroll. The Andalusia/Tariq bin Ziyad subject is distinctly yours and nobody else in your competitor set owns it.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments despite the best reach — the post informs but doesn't ask anything of the viewer. History that just ends as history gets admired, not engaged. Close with a question or a modern lesson ('what would you burn your ships for?') to convert views into comments and saves, like the Tariq-as-mindset reframe in the new ideas.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your highest engagement rate — 45 likes and 5 comments on 369 views. The casual, personal 'never running through a park at night again 😭' caption is relatable and human, and people reward personality. This proves your audience will engage hard when you drop the lecture voice.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's off-pillar — nothing here ties back to leadership, speaking or mindset, so the engagement doesn't build your positioning. Use this relatable, first-person energy as a hook, then bridge into one of your three pillars so the warmth translates into the brand you're actually building.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Clear problem-first framing ('Burnout affects so many of us, whether you're a medical student or not') names a real pain your audience feels, and tying it to a practical tool gives the post a reason to exist beyond motivation.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 209 views with only 2 comments — it reads like a promo for Sabr more than your own take, and audiences scroll past anything that smells like an ad. Lead with your own blunt opinion on burnout (e.g. 'most of your burnout isn't overwork, it's unfinished decisions') and mention the app at the end, not as the premise.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your most-liked post by a mile. Using a hadith to frame a call to action ('Whoever sees an injustice…') plays directly to your audience's values, and the moral clarity ('Silence is not an option') is your voice at its sharpest. This is the proven emotional register for your account.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a Sidecar (image carousel) while every top post across you and all four competitors is Video — you're leaving reach on the table by not putting this conviction to camera. One comment also shows it mobilised feeling but not conversation; end with a concrete 'here's the one thing to do today' so people act and reply, not just double-tap.
